questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The two-hit hypothesis of Knudson applies to:
options: Tumour suppressor genes such as RB1, where both alleles must be inactivated
questions.concept: Tumour suppressor genes are recessive at the cellular level, so both alleles must be lost. In hereditary retinoblastoma one mutation is inherited, so a single somatic hit causes bilateral multifocal tumours at a younger age.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The most commonly mutated gene in human cancers is:
questions.concept: TP53, the guardian of the genome, is mutated in over half of human cancers. It arrests the cell cycle at G1/S for repair or triggers apoptosis; germline loss causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The Philadelphia chromosome is an example of oncogene activation by:
options: Chromosomal translocation creating a fusion gene with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity
questions.concept: t(9;22) fuses BCR to ABL1, producing a constitutively active tyrosine kinase driving chronic myeloid leukaemia - the target of imatinib and the model for targeted cancer therapy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which virus is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.concept: Chronic hepatitis B and C cause cirrhosis with regenerative hyperplasia and genomic instability; HBV additionally integrates into the host genome. Aflatoxin B1 acts synergistically, causing a characteristic TP53 codon 249 mutation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Aflatoxin B1, a chemical carcinogen produced by Aspergillus flavus, causes:
questions.concept: Aflatoxin contaminates improperly stored groundnuts and grains and is a potent hepatocarcinogen, acting synergistically with hepatitis B. Aromatic amines and aniline dyes instead cause bladder cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The Warburg effect in tumour cells refers to:
options: Aerobic glycolysis with high glucose uptake even in the presence of oxygen
questions.concept: Tumours preferentially use glycolysis despite available oxygen, generating biosynthetic intermediates for rapid growth. This underlies FDG-PET imaging, which detects tumours by their avid glucose uptake.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The single most reliable feature distinguishing a malignant from a benign tumour is:
questions.concept: Metastasis unequivocally establishes malignancy; no benign tumour metastasises. Other features - invasion, anaplasia, high mitotic rate, pleomorphism - are suggestive but not absolute.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The commonest route of spread for carcinomas and sarcomas respectively is:
options: Lymphatic for carcinoma and haematogenous for sarcoma
Haematogenous for carcinoma and lymphatic for sarcoma
questions.concept: Carcinomas typically spread first to regional lymph nodes while sarcomas invade veins and spread to lungs, though there are exceptions - follicular thyroid, renal cell and hepatocellular carcinomas spread haematogenously.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition in metastasis involves:
options: Loss of E-cadherin with acquisition of a migratory mesenchymal phenotype
questions.concept: Downregulation of E-cadherin loosens intercellular adhesion, letting carcinoma cells detach, degrade basement membrane with matrix metalloproteinases, intravasate and disseminate. E-cadherin loss is characteristic of diffuse gastric and lobular breast carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Grading of a tumour is based on, and staging on:
options: Degree of differentiation; anatomical extent of spread
questions.concept: Grade reflects histological differentiation and mitotic activity, while stage reflects tumour size, nodal involvement and metastasis by the TNM system. Stage is generally the stronger predictor of prognosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The commonest benign breast tumour in a young woman is:
questions.concept: Fibroadenoma presents in the second and third decades as a firm, smooth, highly mobile painless lump - the breast mouse - with proliferation of both stroma and ducts. It has negligible malignant potential.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The commonest histological type of invasive breast carcinoma is:
options: Invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type
questions.concept: Invasive ductal carcinoma, now called invasive carcinoma of no special type, accounts for about 70 to 80%, forming a hard scirrhous mass with desmoplasia. Lobular carcinoma is often bilateral and multicentric with single-file infiltration from E-cadherin loss.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Peau d'orange appearance of the breast is caused by:
options: Dermal lymphatic obstruction by tumour with tethering at hair follicles
questions.concept: Blocked dermal lymphatics cause dermal oedema, while the skin remains tethered at the follicles producing pitting like orange peel. Extensive peau d'orange without a discrete lump suggests inflammatory carcinoma (T4d).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Paget disease of the nipple is:
options: Eczematous change of the nipple caused by intraepidermal spread of underlying ductal carcinoma
questions.concept: Malignant Paget cells with clear halos infiltrate the nipple epidermis from an underlying in situ or invasive ductal carcinoma. Unlike eczema it starts at the nipple and spreads to the areola, and never resolves with topical steroid.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The most important prognostic factor in breast carcinoma is:
questions.concept: Axillary nodal involvement remains the single strongest prognostic factor, followed by tumour size and grade. Receptor and HER2 status are chiefly predictive of response to endocrine and targeted therapy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Triple-negative breast cancer refers to a tumour negative for:
options: Oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2
questions.concept: Triple-negative tumours cannot be treated with endocrine or anti-HER2 therapy, so chemotherapy is the mainstay. They are commoner in younger women and BRCA1 carriers and have a worse short-term prognosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Fat necrosis of the breast is important because it:
options: Mimics carcinoma clinically and radiologically, often following trauma
questions.concept: Fat necrosis produces a hard irregular mass with skin tethering and calcification that closely mimics malignancy, usually after trauma or surgery. Histology shows lipid-laden macrophages, and biopsy is needed to exclude cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct is most commonly caused by:
questions.concept: An intraductal papilloma in a large lactiferous duct is the commonest cause of single-duct bloody discharge, though carcinoma must be excluded by ductography or microdochectomy with histology.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Comedo-type ductal carcinoma in situ is characterised by:
options: High-grade cells with central necrosis and pleomorphic microcalcification on mammography
questions.concept: Comedo DCIS shows high nuclear grade with central necrosis that calcifies, producing branching pleomorphic microcalcifications on mammography. It carries the highest risk of progression to invasive carcinoma among DCIS subtypes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Gynaecomastia in a male is most often due to:
options: A relative increase in oestrogen to androgen ratio
questions.concept: Physiological gynaecomastia occurs in the newborn, puberty and old age; pathological causes include cirrhosis, Klinefelter syndrome, testicular tumours and drugs such as spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine and ketoconazole.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies are characteristic of:
questions.concept: Papillary carcinoma shows optically clear ground-glass nuclei with grooves and intranuclear inclusions, plus laminated psammoma bodies. Diagnosis rests on these nuclear features, not on papillae, and cytology is diagnostic.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Fine needle aspiration cytology cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because:
options: Malignancy is defined by capsular or vascular invasion, which requires histology of the whole capsule
questions.concept: Both lesions have identical cytological appearances, so the distinction requires demonstration of capsular or vascular invasion in an excised specimen - hence a report of follicular neoplasm mandates diagnostic lobectomy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterised histologically by:
options: Lymphoid follicles with germinal centres and Hurthle (Askanazy) cell change
questions.concept: Autoimmune destruction with anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies produces dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with germinal centres and oxyphilic Hurthle cells. It carries an increased risk of thyroid MALT lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Amyloid stroma in a thyroid tumour indicates:
options: Medullary carcinoma, the amyloid being derived from calcitonin
questions.concept: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells and deposits amyloid derived from procalcitonin, staining with Congo red and showing apple-green birefringence. Serum calcitonin and CEA are markers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: MEN type 1 (Wermer syndrome) comprises tumours of:
questions.concept: MEN1 is the three Ps - parathyroid hyperplasia, pancreatic islet tumours such as gastrinoma and insulinoma, and pituitary adenomas - caused by menin gene mutation. MEN2 involves medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma from RET mutation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: The commonest cause of Cushing syndrome overall is:
questions.concept: Iatrogenic steroid therapy is by far the commonest cause. Among endogenous causes, a pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease) predominates, followed by adrenal tumours and ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome refers to:
options: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage with acute adrenal insufficiency, classically in meningococcaemia
questions.concept: Fulminant meningococcal septicaemia causes disseminated intravascular coagulation with massive bilateral adrenal haemorrhage, producing hypotension, purpura and rapid death unless steroids and antibiotics are given immediately.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Phaeochromocytoma follows the rule of 10s, meaning approximately 10 percent are:
questions.concept: About 10% each are extra-adrenal (paraganglioma, often at the organ of Zuckerkandl), bilateral, malignant, and occur in children; familial cases in MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau and neurofibromatosis are now known to be nearer 25%.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: The commonest cause of primary hypothyroidism worldwide and in India respectively is:
options: Iodine deficiency worldwide and Hashimoto thyroiditis in iodine-sufficient areas
questions.concept: Iodine deficiency remains the leading global cause, though universal salt iodisation has greatly reduced it in India, where autoimmune thyroiditis is now increasingly important in iodine-replete regions.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Endocrine pathology: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, MEN
questions.stem: Nelson syndrome develops after:
options: Bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, with an enlarging ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma and hyperpigmentation
questions.concept: Loss of cortisol feedback after bilateral adrenalectomy allows the corticotroph adenoma to enlarge aggressively, producing mass effects with visual field defects and marked hyperpigmentation from high ACTH and MSH activity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A granuloma is defined as:
options: A focal collection of activated epithelioid macrophages, often with multinucleate giant cells
questions.concept: Granulomas form when macrophages cannot eliminate an agent, transforming into epithelioid cells with abundant pink cytoplasm surrounded by lymphocytes. Th1 cytokines, especially interferon gamma and TNF, drive and maintain them.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Caseating granulomas are most characteristic of:
questions.concept: Central caseous necrosis with a cheesy appearance is typical of tuberculosis, resulting from combined hypersensitivity and mycobacterial lipids. Sarcoidosis, Crohn disease and berylliosis produce non-caseating granulomas.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The Ghon complex in primary pulmonary tuberculosis consists of:
options: A subpleural parenchymal focus with draining hilar lymph node involvement
questions.concept: The Ghon focus lies in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe; with its draining hilar node it forms the Ghon (primary) complex, which usually heals by fibrosis and calcification (Ranke complex).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Secondary (reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis characteristically involves:
options: The apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes
questions.concept: Reactivation favours the apices where oxygen tension is highest and lymphatic drainage poorest, producing cavitation from liquefied caseous material draining into a bronchus - the source of infectivity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Langhans giant cells are distinguished by:
questions.concept: Langhans giant cells, formed by fusion of epithelioid macrophages, have nuclei arranged peripherally in a horseshoe or ring. Foreign body giant cells have haphazardly scattered nuclei, and Touton giant cells a central ring.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Miliary tuberculosis results from:
options: Haematogenous dissemination producing innumerable small uniform granulomas in multiple organs
questions.concept: Erosion of a caseous focus into a blood vessel disseminates bacilli widely, producing millet seed sized lesions in lung, liver, spleen, bone marrow and meninges. It is common in the immunosuppressed and in young children.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Lepromatous leprosy differs from tuberculoid leprosy in having:
options: Numerous bacilli with poor cell-mediated immunity and a negative lepromin test
questions.concept: Lepromatous leprosy reflects a Th2 response with defective cell-mediated immunity, so bacilli are abundant in foamy Virchow cells, lesions are symmetrical and numerous, and the lepromin test is negative. Tuberculoid disease is the opposite pole.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which stain is used to demonstrate Mycobacterium tuberculosis in tissue sections?
questions.concept: The high mycolic acid content of the mycobacterial wall resists acid-alcohol decolourisation after carbol fuchsin staining. Auramine-rhodamine fluorescence is more sensitive for screening large numbers of specimens.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Non-caseating granulomas with asteroid and Schaumann bodies suggest:
questions.concept: Sarcoid granulomas are naked - sparsely surrounded by lymphocytes - and contain stellate asteroid bodies and laminated calcified Schaumann bodies, though neither is specific. Diagnosis requires exclusion of infection.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The gumma of tertiary syphilis is:
options: A granulomatous lesion with central coagulative necrosis and surrounding plasma cell infiltrate
questions.concept: Gummas show central coagulative necrosis with a rim of epithelioid and giant cells and a dense plasma cell infiltrate; obliterative endarteritis with perivascular plasma cells is the histological hallmark of syphilis at all stages.
